title-group.article-title: Low muscle density on chest computed tomography is associated with early death in non–small cell lung cancer

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: The aim of this study was to investigate the association of trunk muscle properties derived from chest computed tomography (CT) with worse posttreatment survival at different follow-up time intervals in patients with non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: This retrospective study included patients with NSCLC who underwent curative resection and postoperative chest CT between March 2020 and April 2021. Cross-sectional area and density of the trunk muscles were measured on CT at the level of the first lumbar vertebra. Cox proportional-hazards models were used to predict worse posttreatment survival risk at different follow-up time intervals adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was calculated to evaluate the diagnostic performance.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 263 patients, 181 died after a median follow-up of 4.1 years. The measured muscle properties were higher in patients who did not die compared with those in patients who died. Patients with high L1 muscle density had lower risks of death within the first year (hazard ratio [HR], 0.58; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.42–0.80; P < 0.01) and overall (HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.63–0.87; P < 0.01). An increase of one standard deviation in L1 muscle density was associated with a 28% lower risk of death after the second year (HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.56, 0.93; P = 0.01). The AUC of L1 muscle density for predicting death within the first year was 0.735.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: There is a time-dependent effect of L1 muscle density on survival in patients with NSCLC. Low L1 muscle density is an important predictor for worse posttreatment survival and is associated with early death.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Lung cancer was the leading cause of cancer death globally in 2022; with an estimated 1.8 million deaths, it accounted for 18.7% of all cancer-related deaths that year [1]. Non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most prevalent histological type of lung cancer. Major improvements in NSCLC treatment have been made owing to advances in targeted therapies and immunotherapies [2]. Despite medical advances, patients often experience alterations in body composition, which may be further exacerbated by the disease and treatments [3, 4]. This wasting condition is known as “cachexia,” and it occurs in 50% of patients with lung cancer [5–7].

Cancer cachexia is a metabolic syndrome that causes ongoing voluntary weight loss, loss of skeletal muscle mass, and decreased muscle strength. It is associated with reduced physical function, poor treatment tolerability, and increased risk of death [7, 8]. Sarcopenia is a sign of cancer-induced cachexia in patients, and it refers to the presence of skeletal muscle depletion [8]. Recently, a meta-analysis reported that patients with sarcopenia have a 1.57-fold higher risk of death and poor overall survival [9, 10]. In addition, patients with sarcopenia exhibit twofold higher risk of death within 30 days after surgery [11]. With the increasing number of lung cancer surgeries, the loss of skeletal muscle has been regarded as an important postoperative prognostic factor beyond tumor-related characteristics [4, 12]. Although considered a well-established indicator of cachexia, weight loss cannot represent all aspects of cachexia and cannot discriminate between fat and muscle mass loss [8]. Thus, comprehensive assessment of skeletal muscle depletion is also needed, and diagnostic tools for cachexia should not only depend on body weight.

Skeletal muscle depletion in patients with cancer is related to both the shrinkage of mass and the decrease in density, the latter of which is characterized by myosteatosis resulting from inter- and intra-muscular fat deposition [4, 13]. Thus, muscle quality may better capture risk factors than the simple quantification of muscle mass. Accurate imaging techniques, such as computed tomography (CT), which are also performed for cancer diagnosis and follow-up, provide unique advantages for the assessment of the mass and density of skeletal muscles [14, 15]. While the level of the third lumbar vertebra is not included in chest CT, the level of the first lumbar vertebral body (L1) is included, and it has been investigated as an alternative level for muscle assessment [16].

The aim of this study was to assess whether muscle properties at the L1 level on chest CT in patients with NSCLC are associated with worse posttreatment survival. In addition, we evaluated which muscle properties could predict worse posttreatment survival at different follow-up time intervals.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This study included a total of 321 consecutive patients diagnosed with primary lung cancer in two hospitals between March 2020 and April 2021, with available chest CT performed within 120–180 days after treatment. All of the patients underwent curative resection as the primary treatment. However, detailed records of specific adjuvant therapies (e.g., chemotherapy regimens, radiotherapy) administered postoperatively and during the follow-up period were not systematically available for the entire cohort. The exclusion criteria were as follows: [1] loss to follow-up (n = 35); [2] diagnosis of small cell lung cancer (n = 11); and [3] CT with severe susceptibility artifacts (n = 12). Finally, 263 patients were enrolled (Fig. 1). The study design and protocol were approved by the ethics committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University (No. JD-HG-2025-006) in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: CT scan acquisition
sec.p: Chest CT was performed in all of the patients using a 256-detector row CT scanner (Brilliance iCT, Philips Healthcare, Cleveland, OH, USA). Scans were acquired from the apical lung to the lower edge of L2. The scanning parameters were as follows: slice thickness, 0.625 mm; slice spacing, 1.25 mm; tube voltage, 120 kVp; automatic tube-current modulation with a mean current of 100 mA; collimator width, 5 mm; and reconstruction matrix, 512 × 512.

sec.title: Assessment of trunk muscle properties
sec.p: The cross-sectional area (cm2) and density (HU) of trunk muscles were measured on a single axial slice at the level of L1 (Fig. 2). The measurements were conducted using OsiriX software (Lite Version 10.0.2, Pixmeo, Geneva, Switzerland). Manual delineation of muscle boundaries was carried out with the “pencil” tool to outline muscle contours. Then, the two-dimensional/three-dimensional segmentation module was applied to semiautomatically select skeletal muscle regions within the predefined HU intensity thresholds (− 30 to 150 HU). Muscle tissue was distinguished from adipose tissue using a threshold of − 29 HU. The trunk muscle area and density values were subsequently calculated [17]. The trunk muscle index (cm2/m2) was derived by dividing the trunk muscle area by the height squared.

caption.p: Measurement of muscle area and muscle of the trunk muscle at the L1 level. A threshold of − 29 to 150 HU was applied to distinguish muscle tissue from fat within the outlining muscle contour

sec.title: Clinical data collection and acquisition of SARC-F
sec.p: Information on demographic characteristics, comorbidities, histological confirmation, and treatment was extracted from the patient’s medical file or medical records in hospital. Vital status up to May 2025 was retrieved from institutional electronic medical records. Patients not documented as deceased were censored as alive at the last date of contact [13].

Trained researchers routinely interviewed patients using the SARC-F questionnaire after chest CT examination. The SARC-F comprises five items, namely strength, assistance with walking, rise from a chair, climb stairs, and fall. Strength was assessed by asking about the difficulty in lifting or carrying 10 lbs. Assistance with walking was evaluated based on the difficulty in walking across a room and whether aids or help were needed. Rising from a chair was determined by asking about the difficulty in transferring from a chair or bed and whether aids or help were needed. Climbing stairs was measured by inquiring about the difficulty in climbing 10 steps. The answers were scored on a scale of 0 (none), 1 (some), and 2 (a lot or unable). Falls were scored a 0 for no falls, 1 for 1–3 falls, and 2 for four or more falls in the past year. Each item was scored from 0 to 2 and then added together. The patients’ total scores ranged from 0 to 10, with higher scores indicating worse physical conditions [18].

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary outcome was overall survival and the number of deaths at different follow-up time intervals. Overall survival was defined as the time from the date of questionnaire acquisition to death from any cause. Secondary outcome was the presence of metastasis at baseline.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed by using SPSS (version 26.0, IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA). Student’s t test was used for continuous variables, whereas the χ2 test or Fisher’s exact test was used for categorical variables. Low trunk muscle area and low trunk muscle index were defined as trunk muscle area and trunk muscle index below sex-specific lower quartile values, respectively. Myosteatosis was identified as a L1 muscle density below 35.5 HU for males and below 32.5 HU for females [18, 19]. Survival curves and cumulative incidence for overall survival within each category based on trunk muscle status were evaluated by using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. To determine the association between trunk muscle properties and survival, hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidential intervals (CIs) were calculated using Cox regression after adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). The proportional hazards assumption for the Cox models was assessed using Schoenfeld residual tests. No significant violations of the assumption were detected for the included variables (all P > 0.05). Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was calculated to determine the diagnostic performance of trunk muscle properties for predicting death at different follow-up intervals. Pairwise comparisons of AUC values between different muscle indicators within the same diagnostic group were performed using the DeLong method. To account for multiple testing and control the false discovery rate, P-values from these pairwise comparisons were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method. A P-value < 0.05 after FDR correction was considered statistically significant. As sex-specific cutoffs were applied for the trunk muscle area and index, and a sex-specific definition was used for myosteatosis, the diagnostic metrics (AUCs) and Cox regression models for these variables were calculated for the entire cohort, inherently accounting for the sex-based adjustments in the initial classification. The selection of the first and second years as time points was based on clinical relevance, as the early postoperative period (particularly the first two years) is widely recognized as a high-risk phase for recurrence and mortality in NSCLC.

sec.title: Clinical characteristics
sec.p: The clinical characteristics of the study are shown in Table 1. Among the 263 patients, there were 164 males and 99 females (mean age, 60.8 ± 10.7 years; range 24–85 years). The median follow-up period was 48.97 months (range, 47.63–61.03 months). A total of 71 patients (27.00%) had a tumor stage of I; 65 patients (24.71%) had a tumor stage of II; and 127 patients (48.29%) had a tumor stage of III or IV. Weight was lower in patients who died than in patients who did not die, especially after the second year. All other demographic-related parameters did not show significant differences. The L1 trunk muscle area, L1 muscle density, and trunk muscle index were lower in patients who died than in those who did not die, particularly within the first year and after the second year. The SARC-F score was higher in patients who died than in those who did not die within the first year.

sec.p: The lowest sex-specific quartiles for the definition of low trunk muscle area were 107.22 cm2 for males and 72.59 cm2 for females. A total of 66 of 263 patients (25.10%) had a low trunk muscle area. The lowest sex-specific quartiles for the definition of low trunk muscle index were 36.82 cm2/m2 for males and 28.33 cm2/m2 for females. A total of 65 of 263 patients (24.71%) had a low trunk muscle index. In total, 145 of 263 patients (55.13%) were identified as having myosteatosis based on the cutoff values of L1 muscle density.

There were no significant effects of muscle properties in discriminating metastasis (Table 2). Table 3 shows that the L1 L1 muscle density was lower in patients who died than in those who did not in both the non-metastasis and metastasis groups.

sec.title: Overall survival
sec.p: In total, 181 of 263 patients (68.82%) died. Death was associated with a low L1 muscle density (log-rank P < 0.01), whereas there was no evidence of an association of death with a low trunk muscle area (log-rank P = 0.27) and a low trunk muscle index (log-rank P = 0.30) (Fig. 3). In the muscle density model, one standard-deviation increase in L1 muscle density was associated with a 26% decreased risk of death (HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.63, 0.87; P < 0.01), with a 42% decreased risk of death within the first year (HR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.42, 0.80; P < 0.01) and a 28% decreased risk of death after the second year (HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.56, 0.93; P = 0.01). There was no evidence of an association of death with the trunk muscle area and trunk density (Table 4).

sec.p: In an exploratory subgroup analysis stratified by sex, the association between low L1 muscle density (myosteatosis) and poor overall survival remained consistent in both male (log-rank P < 0.01) and female (log-rank P = 0.02) patients. The HRs for myosteatosis were comparable between sexes in the multivariate models.

sec.title: Diagnostic performance for the assessment of death
sec.p: The receiver operating characteristic curve and AUC results are shown in Fig. 4; Table 5. For predicting death within the first year, the AUC of L1 muscle density was 0.735 (Fig. 4b), with a sensitivity of 72.60% and a specificity of 63.41%. When discriminating between death within the first year and the second year, L1 muscle density achieved an AUC of 0.758 (Fig. 4d), with a sensitivity of 73.91% and a specificity of 71.23%.

sec.p: Pairwise comparisons using the DeLong method, followed by FDR correction, revealed that in the comparison of “Death within 1st y vs. Death within 2nd y”, the AUC of L1 trunk muscle density (0.758, 95% CI: 0.698–0.818) was significantly higher than that of L1 trunk muscle area (0.619, 95% CI: 0.553–0.685; P = 0.036). Similarly, in the “Death within 1st y vs. no death” group, the diagnostic performance of L1 trunk muscle density (AUC = 0.735, 95% CI: 0.675–0.795) was significantly superior to both L1 trunk muscle area (AUC = 0.639, 95% CI: 0.573–0.705; P = 0.024) and L1 trunk muscle index (AUC = 0.639, 95% CI: 0.573–0.705; P = 0.024). No significant differences in AUC were observed between L1 trunk muscle area and L1 trunk muscle index in any of the comparisons (all P > 0.05 after FDR correction). The performance of muscle properties for the other time interval comparisons is illustrated in Fig. 4e and f and detailed in Table 5.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we evaluated the diagnostic performance of trunk muscle properties for predicting worse posttreatment survival at different follow-up time intervals in patients with NSCLC. Our study demonstrated high diagnostic performance of L1 muscle density for the assessment of worse survival. There was a positive association between L1 muscle density and improved overall survival. No associations between the trunk muscle index and survival or trunk muscle area and survival were observed. In addition, patients with high L1 muscle density were more likely to have a lower risk of death within the first year. These findings suggest that low L1 muscle density is a poor prognostic factor for posttreatment survival, especially within the first year.

We found that low muscle density was associated with death, whereas an increase in L1 muscle density was associated with a decreased risk of early death. The receiver operating characteristic curves further confirmed a stronger discriminative power for mortality risk with the inclusion of L1 muscle density than either. Statistical comparisons confirmed that L1 muscle density exhibited superior diagnostic performance for predicting early death, with significant differences in AUC values compared to other muscle properties after adjustment for multiple testing. The superior predictive value of muscle density over muscle area or index can be mechanistically explained by its direct reflection of muscle quality, specifically the presence of myosteatosis. These results are in line with previous studies, emphasizing the critical role of L1 muscle density in cancer [13, 19–21]. Xiao et al. found that low skeletal muscle density was associated with a substantially higher 30-day mortality risk [20]. According to Sjøblom et al., reduced muscle density reflects high muscle fat content, which is associated with altered metabolism and systemic inflammatory response [21]. Myosteatosis is not merely a marker of volume loss but indicates a pathophysiological state characterized by lipid infiltration within muscle fibers. This condition is closely linked to metabolic dysfunction, including insulin resistance and impaired mitochondrial function, which can exacerbate cancer-associated cachexia and systemic inflammation. Metabolically healthy subjects tend to show a higher proportion of trunk muscles with normal muscle density [19]. Systemic inflammatory response—an independent prognostic marker in cancer in general—is linked to cachexia and may reduce body defense and stimulate growth of neoplasia [22, 23]. The interplay between myosteatosis and a pro-inflammatory state (e.g., elevated cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-α) can create a vicious cycle, further promoting muscle wasting, metabolic dysregulation, and tumor progression, thereby explaining the strong association with early mortality. Furthermore, time-dependent effect of covariates is usually not evaluated, contributing to bias in survival analyses in a previous study [24]; yet, this effect faded within the second year in our study. A possible explanation for this is the low median survival time (35 months) in our study, resulting in low patient numbers. Taken together, information on muscle quality holds potential in oncology practice.

While muscle density has been associated with survival outcomes in patients with NSCLC, the trunk muscle area at L1 and trunk muscle index were not associated with survival in our study. These results are comparable with those of previous studies [13, 21]. Muscle area and index primarily quantify mass but do not differentiate between lean muscle and infiltrated fat. In contrast, muscle density specifically captures the radiodensity of muscle tissue, which decreases with fat accumulation. Therefore, in our cohort, the qualitative deterioration of muscle (myosteatosis) appeared to be a more critical determinant of survival than the quantitative loss of muscle mass alone. Possible reasons could include differences in the extent of surgical resection, other treatments, cancer stage, and overall prognosis. However, some studies have reported that low muscle index is consistently associated with a higher risk of complications and death in other oncological populations [20, 25]. This discrepancy could most likely reflect the milder natural history of other cancers. Another reason could be that several studies that have shown the association between survival and muscle mass may to some extent have overestimated the effect [25]. This may be consistent with studies in older individuals, indicating that muscle density is more strongly associated with muscle strength and physical performance than muscle area [17]. This supports the concept that muscle function and quality, rather than size alone, are paramount for resilience and survival. These results suggest that muscle density may be superior to muscle area and muscle index for predicting survival in some cancer cohorts.

Another interesting aspect of this study is the difference in the SARC-F between those who died within the first year and those who survived, with higher scores associated with worse survival. The SARC-F is a simple screening tool to diagnose sarcopenia in any clinical setting. It requires only five questions with no special equipment, such as a body composition analyzer or dual-energy X-ray absorptiometer. Ueshima et al. reported that higher SARC-F questionnaire scores were associated with increased in-hospital mortality within the first 30 days [26]. Ururi-Cupi et al. stated that higher scores were associated with an increased risk of mortality in older men with cancer [27]. These results demonstrate that sarcopenia increases the risk of mortality, and both cancer and sarcopenia are associated with important complications, such as disability, functional impairment, decreased quality of life, and an increased risk of death [27]. Thus, evaluating the risk of sarcopenia as a risk factor for mortality is vital, especially in cancer.

There are several limitations to our study. First, this was a two-center study with a relatively small number of patients. The results should be confirmed in large-scale population-based prospective studies. Second, we did not have information on dietary intake, perioperative care support, and physical rehabilitation, which may have had an effect on trunk muscle area, L1 muscle density, and outcomes. Moreover, different treatment methods may have an impact on outcomes. Further studies need to explicit it. Third, this study included chest CT after treatment, but it did not include chest CT before treatment, so changes in muscle properties could not be evaluated. Fourth, there were no comprehensive data on adjuvant and subsequent therapies (e.g., specific chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or radiotherapy) received by patients after their initial surgery and during the follow-up period. As these treatments can independently affect both muscle status and survival, their absence from our models is a clear limitation. Fifth, Due to the retrospective design, detailed data on specific comorbidities such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and comprehensive smoking history (e.g., pack-years) were not available for all patients. As these factors can influence systemic inflammation, muscle quality, and prognosis in NSCLC, their absence represents a residual confounding factor that should be considered when interpreting our results. Sixth, The CT scans used for analysis were obtained 120–180 days post-treatment, not at baseline. This introduces a potential survivor bias, as only patients who lived long enough to undergo this follow-up scan were included. Furthermore, muscle status at this timepoint may already reflect the combined effects of the disease and initial treatments, which could complicate the interpretation of its purely prognostic value.

In conclusion, our study indicates that low L1 muscle density is an important poor prognostic factor for worse survival and that it is associated with death after treatment, especially within the first year. This emphasizes the role of a time-dependent effect of L1 muscle density on survival in patients with NSCLC. In the clinic, exercise may be recommended to maintain trunk muscle quality and function, as well as energy balance. This information could be applied to targeted strategies in patient risk stratification and direct interventions to improve muscle quality after treatment to potentially correct adverse conditions.
